common_name: Twickel Purple Lavender (Dutch Heirloom English Lavender)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring or fall in full sun with excellent drainage; Twickel Purple is a true English lavender and, like other Lavandula angustifolia types, is less tolerant of humid summers than lavandin hybrids, so give it maximum air circulation and sharp drainage in the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in full sun with sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil; amend heavy or clay soil with coarse sand or gravel, and avoid overhead watering or mulch touching the crown. Twickel Purple is a long-cultivated Dutch heirloom English lavender, named for the historic Twickel estate in the Netherlands, valued for its compact, tidy, rounded habit and deep violet-purple flower spikes with the classic sweet, floral fragrance and flavor of true English lavender, prized for culinary use, sachets, and potpourri. Because true English lavenders are more prone to root and crown rot in hot, humid conditions than lavandin hybrids, plant Twickel Purple in the driest, sunniest, best-draining spot available and consider it a shorter-lived perennial in the Gulf South compared with more heat-tolerant lavandins like Phenomenal or Grosso. Shear lightly after flowering to maintain shape and prevent the plant from becoming woody and open in the center.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Lavender Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or small plugs in spring in well-drained soil; Elfin Thyme forms an extremely dense, low mat and is often used between stepping stones or as a lawn substitute in small areas, tolerating light foot traffic once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean soil in full sun; Elfin Thyme is one of the smallest and slowest-growing creeping thyme cultivars, forming an extremely dense, tight, mossy-textured mat only an inch or two tall that is prized for planting between stepping stones, in rock garden crevices, and as a miniature lawn substitute in small, well-drained areas. Tiny pink flowers appear in early summer, drawing bees, and the foliage releases a mild thyme fragrance when brushed or lightly stepped on. Because it is slower and more compact than most creeping thymes, it is best used in smaller, well-defined spaces rather than as a large-scale groundcover, where faster-spreading thyme cultivars are more practical. Established plantings are drought-tolerant and need very little care beyond an occasional light shearing after flowering to keep the mat tidy.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Groundcover Thyme Notes

common_name: Doone Valley Thyme (Gold-Variegated Lemon-Scented Creeping Thyme)

planting.note: Plant divisions or small plugs in spring in well-drained soil; Doone Valley is a low, spreading lemon thyme selection with gold-flecked foliage that takes on deeper bronze-red tones in cool weather.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; Doone Valley thyme is a low, mounding, spreading lemon thyme cultivar with dark green leaves speckled and edged in gold that flush deep bronze-red in cool fall and winter weather, giving it strong multi-season ornamental interest beyond its culinary use. The foliage carries a distinct lemony fragrance and flavor, milder and more citrusy than common thyme, and is good for teas, poultry and fish dishes, and infused oils and vinegars. Small pale lilac flowers appear in early summer and attract bees. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and encourage fresh new growth, and avoid heavy, wet soils, which lead to crown rot.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Thyme Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container transplants in spring in well-drained soil; French Thyme is a narrow-leaved, milder-flavored culinary thyme selection favored by cooks for its delicate, refined flavor compared with broader-leaved common thyme.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil; avoid rich, moisture-retentive soil, which shortens the plant's life and dilutes flavor. French Thyme is a narrow, gray-green-leaved culinary thyme selection, distinguished from broader-leaved common thyme by its more delicate texture and milder, sweeter flavor, making it a favorite of classically trained cooks for bouquet garni, herbes de Provence blends, and dishes where a subtler thyme flavor is desired. The small, upright, woody-based subshrub bears tiny pale lavender-pink flowers in early summer that attract bees, and the foliage can be harvested year-round in mild climates, though flavor is best just before flowering. Shear lightly after flowering and again in late summer to keep the plant compact and prevent it from becoming leggy and woody; replace plants every 3-4 years, as thyme naturally declines with age.
sources: Purdue University Extension — Herb Growing Guide
